title: Chapter IX

teacherSummary.text: Mrs. Bennet visits Netherfield with Lydia and Kitty, embarrassing Elizabeth by boasting and mocking Darcy. Lydia demands that Bingley hold a ball.

vocabulary.context: Darcy; the latter of whom, however, could not be prevailed on to join in their censure of her, in spite of all Miss Bingley’s witticisms on fine eyes.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “witticism”: -ism (Greek -ismos, "practice, belief"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To feed and cause to grow
vocabulary.context: Everything nourishes what is strong already.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “nourish”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To pass beyond a limit or boundary
vocabulary.context: We must trespass a little longer on your kindness.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “trespass”: pass (Latin passus, "step"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Pouring forth with fullness or exuberance
vocabulary.context: Bennet was profuse in her acknowledgments.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “profuse”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Darcy only smiled; and the general pause which ensued made Elizabeth tremble lest her mother should be exposing herself again.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “expose”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: An alteration or change for the better
vocabulary.context: In spite of this amendment, however, she requested to have a note sent to Longbourn, desiring her mother to visit Jane, and form her own judgment of her situation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “amendment”: -ment (Latin -mentum, "result or means of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I wonder who first discovered the efficacy of poetry in driving away love!”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “efficacy”: fic (Latin facere, "to make"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: The note was immediately dispatched, and its contents as quickly complied with.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “comply”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bingley for his kindness to Jane, with an apology for troubling him also with Lizzy.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “trouble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Possessing or exhibiting the qualities popularly regarded as belonging to high birth and breeding
vocabulary.context: Bingley—is not he? so much the man of fashion! so genteel and so easy!—He has always something to say to everybody.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “genteel”: gen (Latin/Greek genus, "birth, kind"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: Public behavior reflected on a family's whole reputation in genteel society.

significance: Mrs. Bennet's lack of propriety becomes a real obstacle to her daughters' prospects.
discussionQuestions: How does Mrs. Bennet's behavior hurt the daughters she wants to help?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

items.prompt: Who visits Netherfield to check on Jane?
options: Mrs. Bennet with Lydia and Kitty

items.prompt: How does Elizabeth feel during the visit?
What does Lydia ask Bingley to hold?
How does Mrs. Bennet treat Darcy?

In the line “Darcy; the latter of whom, however, could not be prevailed on to join in their censure of her, in spite of all Miss Bingley’s witticisms on fine eyes.”, what does “witticisms” most nearly mean?
options: To pass beyond a limit or boundary
Pouring forth with fullness or exuberance
To feed and cause to grow

items.prompt: In the line “Everything nourishes what is strong already.”, what does “nourishes” most nearly mean?
options: Pouring forth with fullness or exuberance
To feed and cause to grow
To pass beyond a limit or boundary

answerKey.answer: Mrs. Bennet with Lydia and Kitty
To feed and cause to grow

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter IX,” how does Austen show embarrassing relations? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter IX develops the idea of embarrassing relations. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter IX to complicate the reader's understanding of embarrassing relations. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter IX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of embarrassing relations responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter IX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of embarrassing relations. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: We must trespass a little longer on your kindness.”
satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “trespass” most nearly mean?
options: Possessing or exhibiting the qualities popularly regarded as belonging to high birth and breeding
To pass beyond a limit or boundary

satQuestions.passage: Elizabeth passed the chief of the night in her sister’s room, and in the morning had the pleasure of being able to send a tolerable answer to the enquiries which she very early received from Mr. Bingley by a housemaid, and some time afterwards from the two elegant ladies who waited on his sisters. In spite of this amendment, however, she requested to have a note sent to Longbourn, desiring her mother to visit Jane, and form her own judgment of her situation. The note was immediately dispatched, and its contents as quickly complied with. Mrs. Bennet, accompanied by her two youngest girls, reached Netherfield soon after the family breakfast.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter IX”?
options: A privileged childhood and family love

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: Elizabeth passed the chief of the night in her sister’s room, and in the morning had the pleasure of being able to send a tolerable answer to the enquiries which she very early received from Mr. Bingley by a housemaid, and some time afterwards from the two elegant ladies who waited on his sisters. In spite of this amendment, however, she requested to have a note sent to Longbourn, desiring her mother to visit Jane, and form her own judgment of her situation. The note was immediately dispatched, and its contents as quickly complied with. Mrs. Bennet, accompanied by her two youngest girls, reached Netherfield soon after the family breakfast.

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does Mrs. Bennet's behavior hurt the daughters she wants to help? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are witticisms, nourishes, trespass, profuse, exposing. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Darcy; the latter of whom, however, could not be prevailed on to join in their censure of her, in spite of all Miss Bingley’s witticisms on fine eyes.” Webster's says: A witty saying. Now the word history: “witticism”: -ism (Greek -ismos, "practice, belief"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “nourish”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “trespass”: pass (Latin passus, "step"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Public behavior reflected on a family's whole reputation in genteel society. Why does this chapter matter? Mrs. Bennet's lack of propriety becomes a real obstacle to her daughters' prospects. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to embarrassing relations.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Tone / mood, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Elizabeth passed the chief of the night in her sister’s room, and in the morning had the pleasure of being able to send a tolerable answer to the enquiries which she very early received from Mr. Bingley by a housemaid, and some time afterwards from the two elegant ladies who waited on his sisters. In spite of this amendment, however, she requested to have a note sent to Longbourn, desiring her mother to visit Jane, and form her own judgment of her situation. The note was immediately dispatched, and its contents as quickly complied with. Mrs. Bennet, accompanied by her two youngest girls, reached Netherfield soon after the family breakfast.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Tone / mood, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter IX,” how does Austen show embarrassing relations? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about embarrassing relations, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes embarrassing relations. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
